title: The Bridge with Two Ends
author: Lantern Original
summaryTr: Dere üzerine yapılan yeni köprü, kunduzun düşündüğünden farklı misafirler getirir. Köprünün gerçekten herkese yararlı olması için tek bir hayvanın iyi fikrinden fazlası gerekir.
paragraphs: ## A fine piece of work

In a green valley, a stream ran between two busy places. On one side stood the animals' homes. On the other side were the market, the school, and the common garden. Most animals crossed on a row of large stones. In dry weather, this was easy. After rain, the water covered the lowest stones, and everyone had to take the long path around the hill.

Beaver decided to build a bridge. He liked making things, and he was very good with wood. He measured the stream with a long string. He chose strong branches and cut them to the same length. Every morning, he worked beside the water. Every evening, he checked what he had made. The other animals brought him food and watched the bridge grow.

Rabbit carried carrots to him. Fox brought nails in a little box. Tortoise brought a pot of soup on a low cart. Beaver thanked them all, but he did not ask them many questions. He already had a picture of the bridge in his head. It was straight, wide, and strong. In his picture, everyone crossed it with a smile.

At last, the bridge was ready. Beaver made a sign and hung it above the entrance. It said, 'A bridge for everyone.' He invited the whole valley to come on Sunday morning. He cleaned the wooden boards, put flowers beside the posts, and stood in the middle. He was tired, but he was also proud. The long walk around the hill was over.

Rabbit arrived first. She jumped onto the bridge and ran to the other side. Fox followed her, carrying his box. Deer crossed slowly and looked down at the water. The boards did not move. Everyone clapped. Beaver bowed so low that his nose almost touched the wood. Then Tortoise came up the path with her empty soup cart and stopped at the first step.

The step was high. Tortoise put one front foot on it, then the other. She could lift herself, but she could not pull the cart after her. Beaver hurried over. 'I will carry it,' he said. He lifted the cart onto the bridge. Tortoise climbed up slowly. At the other end, there was another high step. Beaver carried the cart down again.

'Thank you,' said Tortoise. 'Will you be here tomorrow morning?' Beaver looked surprised. 'I must collect wood tomorrow.' 'And on Tuesday?' she asked. 'I have work then too.' Tortoise nodded. 'I go to the garden every day. My cart goes with me.' Beaver looked at his fine sign. The words were clear, but suddenly he was not sure about them.
## One good answer

That afternoon, Beaver made a long wooden board for each entrance. The boards went from the ground to the bridge like gentle hills. He asked Tortoise to try them. She pulled her cart up one board, crossed the bridge, and went down the other. This time, she did not need help. Beaver smiled. 'Now it is a bridge for everyone,' he said.

On Monday, Mouse came from the market with a bag of seeds. She was very small, and the spaces between the bridge boards were wide for her feet. She crossed slowly, looking down at every step. In the middle, one seed fell from her bag and dropped through a space. Mouse sat beside the rail until Rabbit arrived and walked across with her.

Beaver was sorry when he heard about this. He took some thin pieces of wood and covered the spaces along one side. Mouse tried the new narrow path. Her feet stayed on the wood, and her seed bag stayed beside her. 'That is much better,' she said. Beaver wrote a small note in his notebook. He wanted to remember the size of her feet.

Then Duck came with six little ducks. They liked the new bridge because the water was cold that morning. But at the far end, the wide board was wet and smooth. One little duck sat down suddenly and slid to the bottom. She was not hurt, but she was angry. All five of her brothers and sisters wanted to slide too. Duck wanted to reach school.

Beaver added small wooden strips across the wide boards. Now wet feet could hold them better. Duck tested the entrance before bringing the little ducks again. They walked down without sliding. One of them looked disappointed. Beaver nearly laughed, but he kept quiet. A bridge could not be both a good school path and a good slide at the same time.

By Wednesday, Beaver had worked on the bridge for three extra days. He sat under a tree with his notebook. There were drawings of feet, wheels, and wooden strips on every page. Fox found him there. 'It was such a simple bridge,' Beaver said. 'Now every animal has a new problem.' Fox sat beside him. 'Perhaps the problems were here before the bridge,' he said.

Beaver did not like that answer at first. He had worked hard. The bridge was strong, and most animals could cross it easily. But then he thought of Tortoise's cart. She had not made it difficult on purpose. It was simply her cart, and she needed it. Mouse had not chosen small feet to trouble him. He opened his notebook to a fresh page.
## The meeting in the middle

On Thursday, Beaver invited the animals to a meeting. He put a table in the middle of the bridge. 'Tell me what this bridge needs,' he said. At once, everyone began to speak. Rabbit wanted a straight running path. Mouse wanted a quiet corner. Deer wanted higher rails. Duck wanted a low rail so the little ducks could see the water. Fox wanted space for a market stall.

Beaver tried to write everything. Soon his pencil broke. Tortoise, who had arrived last, waited until the others were quiet. 'Why is the table on the bridge?' she asked. 'For our meeting,' said Beaver. 'Yes,' she said. 'But Hedgehog is behind me with a basket. He wants to cross, and we are in his way.' Everyone turned around. Hedgehog waved politely.

They moved the meeting under the tree. Hedgehog crossed with his basket. Beaver found another pencil. 'Let us try again,' he said. 'Tell us about a time when you need to cross.' This question brought different answers. Rabbit carried fresh bread before breakfast. Mouse returned from the market in the afternoon. Deer crossed at night after visiting her mother. Tortoise took heavy vegetables home slowly.

As they listened, the animals stopped asking for everything at once. Rabbit did not need to run all day. Deer did not need a higher rail if she could see the edges clearly at night. Duck wanted to see the water, but she also wanted her children to stay safe. Fox admitted that his stall could stand near the bridge instead of on it.

Mouse drew a line on the ground with a stick. 'What if the quiet path stays on one side?' she asked. 'The wider part can be for carts and larger feet.' Rabbit looked at the line. She could still carry her bread across. She only needed to slow down when someone else was there. It was not her first choice, but it was possible.

They agreed to try a plan for one week. Beaver would mark the edges with pale paint. Mouse would help make a clear line beside the narrow path. Fox would put his stall on the market side, well away from the entrance. Rabbit would walk across when the bridge was busy. Tortoise would test every change with her cart. Duck would bring a bucket of water to test the wet boards.

For the first time, Beaver did not work alone. Deer carried the paint. Rabbit cleaned the boards. Mouse checked the smallest spaces. Fox held the tools, although he sometimes offered advice when nobody asked for it. By evening, the bridge looked less like Beaver's first drawing. It also looked more like a place the whole valley used. Beaver could not decide how he felt about that.
## The red ribbon

The next morning, Fox opened his market stall. He sold string, baskets, and three kinds of buttons. To help customers find him, he tied a long red ribbon to a post near the bridge. The ribbon moved beautifully in the wind. By midday, several animals had bought things. Fox was pleased. Then a strong wind blew the ribbon across the entrance, directly in front of Tortoise.

Tortoise stopped her cart. Behind her, Duck stopped with the little ducks. Behind Duck, Deer waited with a bag of flour. Rabbit came from the other side with an empty bread basket. She saw the line and called to Fox. He ran over and lifted the ribbon. Everyone moved again. 'It was only a decoration,' he said. Tortoise looked at the full path behind her.

That evening, the animals met under the tree again. Beaver was ready to make another rule, but Mouse raised her paw. 'Can we ask the new question?' she said. Fox sighed. 'I need customers to see my stall.' Rabbit pointed to his plain brown sign. 'We can paint that red. A sign will not blow across the path.' Fox thought about it and agreed.

They painted the sign together. Fox took the ribbon down and cut it into short pieces to tie around small bags of buttons. He sold two bags the next morning. 'The ribbon still has a job,' he told Tortoise. 'It simply has a different place.' Tortoise bought some strong string for her cart. She did not mention the long wait at the bridge.

On the fourth day of the trial, rain fell from morning until evening. Beaver worried about the new paint, but it stayed on the wood. Mouse crossed safely along her narrow path. Duck's family did not slide. Tortoise could pull her cart up both entrances. Everything seemed right. Then Deer arrived at the market side with her mother, who walked slowly and needed frequent rests.

There was nowhere to sit near that end of the bridge. The nearest bench was across the water. Deer's mother could make the crossing, but first she needed to rest. Fox brought a strong wooden box from his stall. She sat on it and thanked him. When Beaver arrived, he looked at the box. 'We have worked on the bridge,' he said, 'but we forgot the places beside it.'
## The other end

Beaver walked from one end to the other with his notebook. On the home side, the path was smooth and there was a bench under the tree. On the market side, the ground was rough and baskets stood near the entrance. He had always started from his own home. For him, the bridge began with a comfortable place. For other animals, it began somewhere different.

He asked Deer and her mother to walk with him. He did not carry tools this time. He listened while they showed him where a bench could stand without blocking anyone. Then he asked Tortoise to bring her cart from the market. One wheel caught between two stones before she reached the bridge. It was a small problem, but it happened every day.

The animals spent Saturday morning improving both paths. They moved the baskets, filled the space between the stones, and built a second bench. Beaver showed Rabbit how to smooth the wood. Fox brought warm drinks. Mouse made a little seat beside the large bench, because the large one was too high for her. Nobody called it a special seat. It was simply another seat.

At the end of the week, they met again. Beaver read out the changes from his notebook. There were more than he expected. Some were made of wood or paint. Others were small agreements about how to use the bridge. Rabbit looked embarrassed when he mentioned walking. 'I forgot once,' she said. Mouse nodded. 'You stopped when I called.' Rabbit promised to keep trying.

'Is it finished now?' asked Fox. Beaver looked at the bridge. It was strong, useful, and busy. Two little ducks were crossing with their school bags. Tortoise waited for them before taking her cart onto the wide path. On the far side, Deer's mother was sitting in the sun. Beaver thought about Fox's question. A week earlier, he had known the answer immediately.

'The building work is finished for now,' he said. 'But we can still listen.' He put his notebook in a small wooden box under the tree. Anyone could leave a drawing or a message there. Mouse could not reach the top of the box, so Beaver lowered it before anyone asked. Tortoise smiled when she saw him do that. Beaver smiled back.

That night, Beaver took down his first sign. The words 'A bridge for everyone' were still bright. He did not throw it away. He painted a smaller line beneath them: 'Tell us how you cross.' In the morning, he hung it where animals coming from either direction could read it. The sign was no longer a promise he had made alone. It was also an invitation.

A few days later, a young Otter arrived in the valley. She looked at the bridge, the two paths, and the benches. 'Who built all this?' she asked. Rabbit pointed to Beaver, who was carrying his tools home. Beaver stopped when he heard her. 'I built the first bridge,' he said. 'Then we learned where its two ends really were.' He went home by the market path, just to see it again.

quiz.q: What is Tortoise's first problem with the bridge?
options: The steps are too high for her cart
She is afraid of the paint
quiz.explainTr: İlk köprünün giriş ve çıkışındaki yüksek basamaklar, kaplumbağanın arabasını tek başına geçirmesine engel olur.

quiz.q: Why do the animals move their meeting under the tree?
quiz.explainTr: Köprü üzerindeki toplantı, sepetiyle karşıya geçmek isteyen kirpinin yolunu kapatır.

quiz.q: What replaces Fox's long red ribbon?
quiz.explainTr: Tavşanın önerisiyle tezgâhın kahverengi tabelası kırmızıya boyanır; uçuşan kurdele kaldırılır.

quiz.q: What does Beaver notice when Deer's mother needs a rest?
options: The market end has no nearby seat
quiz.explainTr: Geyiğin annesi dinlenmek isteyince kunduz, pazar tarafında oturacak yakın bir yer olmadığını fark eder.

quiz.q: Why does Beaver add 'Tell us how you cross' to the sign?
options: He wants every animal to pay
He wants to keep learning about different needs
He wants to close the bridge
He wants only fast animals to cross
quiz.explainTr: Yeni yazı, hayvanların farklı ihtiyaçlarını anlatmaları için bir davettir; kunduz dinlemeye devam etmek ister.
